I already had the layers on paper. [PAVED](/blog/building-a-platform) names them, [the operating-model write-up](/blog/platform-engineering) argues why they exist, and [Kratix](/blog/kratix) is the thing that implements most of them on Kubernetes. What I didn't have was a version I could hold in my head without a cluster.

So I built one. Python, a directory of JSON files, one capability: a developer asks for an application environment and gets a namespace, a running app, a URL, a database, and a dashboard stub as a single request. No Kubernetes, no Docker, no Vault. The data plane is fake on purpose. The control plane is not.

I wasn't trying to ship an IDP. I wanted to know if the layers still hold when you can't hide behind CRDs. They do. The tools change. The sequencing doesn't.

Each section is the Python that implements a layer, then the one production tool I'd actually use instead of keeping the Python. The shopping list is already in the PAVED post. This is the afternoon proving the shopping list isn't the architecture.

The code is at [github.com/richpeaua/platform-from-scratch](https://github.com/richpeaua/platform-from-scratch):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/richpeaua/platform-from-scratch.git
cd platform-from-scratch
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

## The request

Same contract as the PAVED example. Outcome-shaped, not infra-shaped:

```yaml
apiVersion: platform/v1
kind: AppEnvironment
metadata:
  name: checkout
spec:
  team: payments
  tier: production
  image: checkout:1.4.2
  domain: checkout.acme.io
  components:
    database: postgres
    cache: true
  observability: true
```

No instance class. No storage size. No Postgres version. `database: postgres` is the whole ask. HA, backups, and credential minting happen behind that field, in a nested capability the developer never writes.

```bash
platform apply -f examples/checkout-env.yaml
platform get appenvironment checkout
```

```yaml
status:
  phase: Ready
  url: https://checkout.acme.io
  db_secret_ref: environments/checkout/database/credentials
```

That's the whole thing working. The rest of this post is how it got there.

Build order is 0, then P, then V, then E, then A, then D. You expose the reverse. I already argued that in the PAVED post; I'm not going to re-argue it. I'm going to show the code.

## Layer 0: something has to store state

Every layer above this needs the same four things: a place to keep desired state, a single door that writes go through, a way for controllers to look at the world, and a split between what was requested (`spec`) and what actually exists (`status`). Skip this and every capability invents its own store, its own validation hook, its own idea of "ready." They drift. That's how you get six platforms.

Kubernetes bundles this as etcd plus the API server. I didn't use Kubernetes. I used JSON files:

```
data/resources/{group}/{kind}/{namespace}/{name}.json
```

The store is dumb. Get, list, write, delete. Dumb is the point. Intelligence lives in controllers.

The interesting bit is the hub. Every mutation goes through it: human apply, controller status write, child resource emission. One door.

```python
class Hub:
    def apply(self, resource_dict: dict, *, skip_admission: bool = False) -> Resource:
        if not skip_admission and self.admission is not None:
            resource_dict = self.admission.admit(resource_dict)
        resource = Resource.from_dict(resource_dict)
        existing = self.store.get(...)
        if existing:
            resource.status = existing.status  # keep observed state on spec update
        return self.store.write(resource)

    def update_status(self, resource: Resource) -> Resource:
        return self.store.write(resource)
```

When someone re-applies a changed spec, the hub keeps the old status. Humans write desired state. Controllers write observed state. That's how you stop a developer from forging `phase: Ready`.

The object itself is boring on purpose:

```python
class Resource(BaseModel):
    apiVersion: str
    kind: str
    metadata: Metadata
    spec: dict[str, Any] = Field(default_factory=dict)
    status: dict[str, Any] = Field(default_factory=dict)
```

Metadata carries `owner_references`, `finalizers`, `deletion_timestamp`. Status carries conditions: `{type, status, reason, message}`. Same shape Kubernetes uses, minus the cluster.

**Production: kind.** Don't rebuild this layer. Stand up a cluster and inherit the machinery.

```bash
kind create cluster --name paved-dev
kubectl get nodes
# NAME                       STATUS   ROLES           AGE
# paved-dev-control-plane    Ready    control-plane   30s
```

Locally that's kind. In prod that's EKS, GKE, or AKS. Multi-cluster is Cluster API or Karmada if you actually need it. The bill for skipping Kubernetes is rebuilding reconciliation, admission, typed APIs, and garbage collection yourself, which is what this Python is. Fine for a weekend. Not fine for a company.

## Layer P: a contract that doesn't leak how

Federation only works if teams integrate against a schema, not each other's Terraform. Three properties, none of them optional:

- The request states the outcome (`tier: production`), not the procedure (`run module v3.2`).
- Bad requests die at submission, not in a pipeline at 2am.
- The producer can rewrite the implementation. Consumers don't notice.

Type first, behavior later. A CRD with no controller is typed storage. That's this layer.

I registered types as Pydantic models. `AppEnvironment` is the public contract:

```python
class AppEnvironmentSpec(BaseModel):
    team: str
    tier: Tier                          # dev | staging | production
    image: str
    domain: str | None = None
    components: ComponentsSpec = ...    # database: none|postgres|mysql
    observability: bool = True
```

What's missing is the whole argument. No `storage_gb`. No `instance_class`. No `postgres_version`. Those live on a nested `Database` type the environment controller emits:

```python
class DatabaseSpec(BaseModel):
    engine: DatabaseKind
    ha: bool = False
    backups: bool = False
    storage_gb: int = 20
```

The developer never writes a Database. Change HA defaults, swap vendors, rewrite the controller: the AppEnvironment schema doesn't move.

`platform explain appenvironment` dumps the fields, enums, and defaults. Apply a bad tier and it never reaches a controller:

```yaml
spec:
  team: payments
  tier: prod          # not in the enum
  image: app:1.0.0
```

```bash
platform apply -f bad-tier.yaml
# schema validation failed: ...
```

**Production: a CRD.** Same schema, now a real API:

```yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: appenvironments.platform.acme.io
spec:
  group: platform.acme.io
  names:
    kind: AppEnvironment
    plural: appenvironments
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
    - name: v1
      served: true
      storage: true
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                team:   { type: string }
                tier:   { type: string, enum: ["dev", "staging", "production"] }
                image:  { type: string }
                domain: { type: string }
                components:
                  type: object
                  properties:
                    database: { type: string, enum: ["none", "postgres", "mysql"], default: "none" }
                    cache:    { type: boolean, default: false }
                observability: { type: boolean, default: true }
              required: [team, tier, image]
      subresources:
        status: {}
```

```bash
kubectl apply -f appenvironment-crd.yaml
kubectl explain appenvironment.spec.components.database
```

Still no controller. Malformed requests already bounce. Crossplane XRDs and Kratix Promise `.spec.api` blocks are the same idea with extra wrapping. Kubebuilder generates this from Go types if you'd rather not hand-write OpenAPI.

## Layer V: make the ask real, then keep it real

A contract with no fulfillment is a validated notebook. This layer binds it to the world and keeps binding it. Level-triggered, not fire-and-forget: list everything you own, reconcile each object against current spec, repeat. Crash during a run and the next pass re-derives the gap. Pipelines check at commit time. Controllers check continuously.

```python
def reconcile_all(self) -> None:
    # two passes so children exist before the parent reads their status
    for _ in range(2):
        for kind, controller in self._controllers.items():
            for resource in self.store.list(kind=kind):
                controller.reconcile(resource)
```

The AppEnvironment controller fans one object into a tree:

```
AppEnvironment "checkout"
  ├─ Environment      namespace + quota
  ├─ App              image → compose file + port
  ├─ Ingress          domain → https URL
  ├─ Database         nested capability, separate controller
  └─ Observability    dashboard stub
```

Each child is a resource with an owner reference:

```python
child_dict = {
    "apiVersion": "platform/v1",
    "kind": "Database",
    "metadata": {
        "name": name,
        "ownerReferences": [owner_ref(owner)],
    },
    "spec": DatabaseSpec(engine=db_kind, ha=ha, backups=backups).model_dump(),
}
```

The Database controller is its own loop. It picks storage size, writes credentials to disk, reports `secret_ref`. Nobody asked for `storage_gb: 20`. They asked for postgres.

Status goes back through the hub:

```python
status.phase = "Ready"
status.conditions = set_condition(
    status.conditions, "Ready", "True", "Provisioned",
    f"Environment ready at {url}",
)
self.hub.update_status(resource)
```

Delete uses a finalizer. `platform delete appenvironment checkout` stamps `deletion_timestamp` and leaves the object sitting there until the controller tears down children and disk artifacts, then drops the finalizer. Only then does the object actually vanish. That's the difference between "I sent a delete" and "the database is gone."

Apply twice. Same URL, same phase. If the second apply did something different, the loop isn't level-triggered, it's just a script that remembers.

No containers run. Compose files and credential JSON land on disk. I care about the control loop, not whether Postgres actually started.

**Production: Kubebuilder.** Same loop, real objects:

```go
func (r *AppEnvironmentReconciler) Reconcile(ctx context.Context, req ctrl.Request) (ctrl.Result, error) {
    var env platformv1.AppEnvironment
    if err := r.Get(ctx, req.NamespacedName, &env); err != nil {
        return ctrl.Result{}, client.IgnoreNotFound(err)
    }
    if err := r.ensureNamespace(ctx, &env); err != nil {
        return ctrl.Result{}, err
    }
    if env.Spec.Components.Database != "none" {
        if err := r.ensurePostgreSQLClaim(ctx, &env); err != nil {
            return ctrl.Result{}, err
        }
    }
    env.Status.Phase = "Ready"
    env.Status.URL = "https://" + env.Spec.Domain
    return ctrl.Result{}, r.Status().Update(ctx, &env)
}
```

That claim is someone else's problem. Crossplane Composition or a Kratix Promise sizes it, adds HA, takes backups. The environment controller never learned what `db.r6g.large` means.

Ship the controller through kuttl or envtest, sign the image with cosign, let Argo CD (or Flux) apply what it emits. Terraform and Pulumi still belong here if a leaf is cloud-shaped; they run *inside* the loop, they are not the loop.

In production the fan-out looks like this:

```
AppEnvironment "checkout"
  ├─ Namespace + ResourceQuota + NetworkPolicy
  ├─ Deployment + HPA
  ├─ Ingress + cert-manager Certificate
  ├─ PostgreSQL claim → Crossplane / Kratix
  ├─ Redis, if cache: true
  ├─ ExternalSecret ← Vault
  ├─ Grafana dashboard + Prometheus rules
  └─ Argo CD Application
```

Same tree as the Python. The leaves are real.

## Layer E: rails before on-ramps

Self-service without policy is a portal over a ticket queue. Everyone can request anything, so someone still has to look. Put the rails up first. Then opening the on-ramps is boring, which is the goal.

Admission runs on every write through the hub. Schema, then defaults, then policy. Fail before persist.

```python
def admit(self, resource: dict) -> dict:
    validated_spec = definition.validate_spec(spec)
    resource = {**resource, "spec": validated_spec}
    for policy in self.policies:
        policy(resource)
    return resource
```

Three rules, all the ones from the PAVED write-up:

```python
ALLOWED_TEAMS = {"payments", "platform", "checkout", "identity"}

def validate_team(resource):
    team = resource.get("spec", {}).get("team")
    if team not in ALLOWED_TEAMS:
        raise AdmissionError(f"team '{team}' is not in allowlist")

def validate_domain_zone(resource):
    domain = resource.get("spec", {}).get("domain")
    if domain and not domain.endswith(".acme.io"):
        raise AdmissionError(f"domain '{domain}' must be under *.acme.io")

def validate_production_no_latest(resource):
    if spec.get("tier") == "production":
        if image.endswith(":latest") or ":" not in image:
            raise AdmissionError("production requires a pinned image tag")
```

Admission can't express everything. Production environments force database HA and backups in the *controller*, regardless of the request:

```python
ha = spec.tier == Tier.PRODUCTION
backups = spec.tier == Tier.PRODUCTION
DatabaseSpec(engine=db_kind, ha=ha, backups=backups)
```

The developer doesn't have a field for that. They also don't have a way around it.

Break the policies. `team: rogue-squadron` dies at the allowlist. `checkout.evil.com` dies at the zone check. `checkout:latest` on production dies at the pin. None of them leave a half-built environment on disk. That's the difference between a guardrail and a linter in CI that someone skipped.

**Production: Kyverno.** Same `:latest` rule, now at the API server:

```yaml
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: appenvironment-production-guardrails
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
    - name: no-latest-in-production
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: [AppEnvironment]
      preconditions:
        all:
          - key: "{{ request.object.spec.tier }}"
            operator: Equals
            value: production
      validate:
        message: "production requires a pinned image tag"
        pattern:
          spec:
            image: "!*:latest"
    - name: domain-must-be-acme
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: [AppEnvironment]
      validate:
        message: "domain must be under *.acme.io"
        pattern:
          spec:
            domain: "*.acme.io"
```

```bash
kubectl apply -f checkout-env-bad.yaml
# Error from server: admission webhook "validate.kyverno.io" denied the request:
# production requires a pinned image tag
```

Gatekeeper and CEL ValidatingAdmissionPolicy do the same job. Vault plus External Secrets Operator handles the credential side. OpenCost watches the budget. The property that matters is *where* they run: at the hub, once, for every on-ramp. Not in each team's pipeline.

## Layer A: more than one door, same road

The contract is *what*. This layer is *how*. CLI, form, Terraform module, `kubectl` - all of them have to submit the same object and hit the same policies. A second path around the hub is a second platform you will forget to secure.

The Python has a CLI. That's it. Apply, get, list, explain, delete, catalog. Apply is thin on purpose:

```python
@cli.command()
def apply(files):
    for path in files:
        data = yaml.safe_load(path.read_text())
        resource = platform.apply(data)
        click.echo(f"{resource.kind}/{resource.metadata.name} applied")
```

It does not talk to the store. It does not skip admission. It's a door.

```bash
platform apply -f examples/checkout-env.yaml
platform get appenvironment checkout
platform delete appenvironment checkout
```

Delete is where you feel the finalizer. The object sits in Terminating until children are gone.

**Production: kubectl.** Same YAML, different door:

```bash
kubectl apply -f examples/checkout-env.yaml
kubectl get appenvironment checkout -o yaml
# status:
#   phase: Ready
#   url: https://checkout.acme.io
```

Then you add the other doors. A Backstage Software Template that emits this object. A Terraform module that POSTs it. Port if that's what the org already bought. Score or Radius if you want a workload spec that compiles down to the same CR. Three interfaces, one contract, one Kyverno policy, one Kubebuilder controller.

The failure mode is the "just for now" portal that writes RDS directly. Now you have two platforms.

## Layer D: if they can't find it, it doesn't exist

Last because there's nothing to catalog until something is built, guarded, and reachable. A pile of independently-owned capabilities is not a platform until someone can search "new app" and get a name, an owner, and a button.

Two lists. Capabilities: the menu. Instances: things that actually got provisioned. The AppEnvironment controller registers an instance when status hits Ready. No extra sync job.

```python
CapabilityEntry(
    name="app-environment",
    title="Application Environment",
    description="Self-service production-ready environment",
    owner="team-platform",
    lifecycle="production",
    tags=["environment", "app", "self-service"],
)
```

```bash
platform catalog list
# app-environment   Application Environment   owner=team-platform
# app-environment/checkout   https://checkout.acme.io   owner=payments

platform catalog search "self-service"
```

Owner is the field people skip. A catalog without owners is a directory of tickets.

**Production: Backstage.** A `catalog-info.yaml` next to the CRD docs:

```yaml
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: app-environment
  title: Application Environment
  description: Self-service production-ready environment for a service.
  tags: [platform, self-service, environment]
  links:
    - url: https://docs.acme.io/platform/app-environment
      title: How to launch an environment
    - url: https://backstage.acme.io/create/templates/app-environment
      title: Launch an environment
spec:
  type: platform-capability
  lifecycle: production
  owner: team-platform
```

The launch link is the Layer A template. TechDocs renders the tier docs. When an environment goes Ready, a plugin registers the instance and hangs Grafana and Argo CD off it. Port, Cortex, OpsLevel - same job, different vendor. Pick one and put an owner on every entry.

## One request, both stacks

Python:

```
CLI reads YAML
  → admission: schema, team, domain, :latest
  → hub writes spec
  → AppEnvironment controller emits children
  → Database controller mints credentials
  → status: Ready, URL, secret ref
  → catalog registers the instance
```

Production:

```
kubectl / Backstage / Terraform
  → Kyverno + CRD schema
  → etcd
  → Kubebuilder reconciler
      namespace, Deployment, Ingress, cert-manager
      PostgreSQL claim → Crossplane
      ExternalSecret ← Vault
  → .status
  → Backstage instance
```

Same sequence. Different machinery.

If I threw the Python away tomorrow, I'd keep the contract, the child-resource split, the admission-before-CLI ordering, and the catalog-last rule. I'd swap the store for a cluster, the Pydantic models for a CRD, the reconcilers for Kubebuilder, the policy functions for Kyverno, the CLI for kubectl plus a template, the dict-in-a-file catalog for Backstage.

## What's fake

The control plane is real: spec/status, admission, reconcilers, finalizers, nested capabilities, catalog on Ready, tests that cover the happy path and the policy rejects.

The data plane is not. Compose files instead of Deployments. A URL string instead of cert-manager. JSON credentials instead of Vault. CLI only. I ran pytest, applied the example by hand, and caught one bug where `apply` returned status from before reconcile finished. That's the verification. Not a security review, not concurrent-write tests, not CI.

That's enough to feel why the layers exist. It is not enough to run a company on.

I already knew the tools. Building the dumb version is what made the tools make sense.
